title: Radiation protection in the practice
blurb: The controlled area, where staff stand, warning signs, protecting the patient with collimation and holders, lead aprons and thyroid collars, pregnancy, and faulty equipment.
question: The dentist is about to take a periapical and a new nurse stays beside the chair 'to help the patient keep still'. The patient, who mentions she might be pregnant, asks for a lead apron. Afterwards you notice the tubehead slowly drifting down. What should happen in each case?

teach.body: Everyone near an X-ray set is protected by three simple ideas: time, distance and shielding. Keep exposures short and few, keep people as far from the tubehead and patient as possible, and put walls or barriers in the way. In the surgery this becomes a defined controlled area that only the patient should be inside during an exposure, warning signs and lights, and techniques that keep the patient's own dose as low as reasonably practicable.

When the X-ray set is switched on and ready to expose, a controlled area exists. Many practices designate the whole room (option A). Where that isn't practicable, it is everywhere within 1.5 metres of the tubehead and patient in any direction, plus the path of the primary beam until it has been sufficiently absorbed (option B). For CBCT the whole room is the only recommended option. Staff must leave the controlled area for every exposure and press the button from outside it.

items.label: controlled area boundary from tubehead and patient (option B)
annual employee dose limit; dental staff doses sit well below 1 mSv
patient dose saved by rectangular rather than round collimation
minimum focus-to-skin distance from the spacer cone

teach.caption: Equipment has a 'mains on' light and an 'X-rays' light that shows while X-rays are being produced. The operator must be able to see the patient throughout the exposure.

levels.label: PPE
levels.sub: Only where the risk assessment needs it

teach.h: Protecting the patient vs protecting staff

teach.body: Lead aprons are not justified routinely for any dental radiograph, including for pregnant patients. The beam is never aimed at the abdomen, and an apron can't stop the scatter that arises inside the patient's head. Thyroid collars are not routine either: good technique and collimation protect the thyroid more. A collar is only used, on the MPE's advice, when the thyroid would unavoidably be in the primary beam, for example an upper standard occlusal or some CBCT and ceph views.

rows.label: Tell the dentist so they can review justification

teach.note: IR(ME)R requires an employer's procedure for asking about pregnancy (ages 12–55) where relevant. In dentistry the primary beam doesn't reach the pelvis, so it rarely changes the decision, but the dentist must be told.

steps.label: Switch off
steps.sub: At the mains or emergency stop

steps.label: Report
steps.sub: To the RPS or dentist; follow contingency plan

teach.caption: This applies to a tubehead that drifts, a damaged unit, a warning light that stays on, or an exposure that won't stop.

teach.text: Never hold the receptor, the tubehead or the patient during an exposure. Staff are strongly discouraged from staying in the controlled area. If a patient needs support, a carer or comforter may help under a separate justification.

items: Controlled area: whole room, or 1.5 m from tubehead and patient plus the primary beam.
Staff leave the controlled area; anyone who must stay keeps as far back as possible, out of the beam.
Rectangular collimation, holders and the paralleling technique cut patient dose.
No routine lead aprons or thyroid collars. Faulty equipment: stop, switch off, label, report.

summary: You can now describe the controlled area, explain where staff stand and why, recognise warning signs, list the measures that protect patients and staff, explain why aprons and thyroid collars aren't routine, handle a possible pregnancy correctly, and respond safely to faulty equipment.

A.q: Using option B, how far from the tubehead and patient does the controlled area extend for an intraoral X-ray set?
A.why: Option B defines the controlled area as within 1.5 m of the tubehead and patient in any direction, plus the primary beam.

whyNot.0: 0.5 m would leave staff far too close to the source.
whyNot.1: 1 metre is not the distance given in the UK guidance.
whyNot.2: 3 metres is further than the defined boundary, although standing further away is always safer.

A.q: A patient asks why she isn't given a lead apron for her bitewings. What is the best explanation?
options: The beam never aims at the abdomen
The practice has run out of aprons
A.why: The primary beam is never directed at the abdomen, and an apron can't stop scatter inside the head, so aprons aren't routinely justified.

whyNot.0: Aprons aren't routinely used for children either.
whyNot.2: Aprons are outside the beam and don't affect image density.
whyNot.3: Aprons are not routinely needed at all, so availability isn't the reason.

A.q: You notice the tubehead drifting downwards after positioning. What should you do?
options: Hold it steady during the exposure
Prop it up with a cotton roll
Stop using it and report it
Use it until the next service
A.why: A drifting or damaged tubehead must be taken out of use and reported so it can be repaired; no one should hold or improvise.

whyNot.0: Holding the tubehead would put your hand in or near the beam.
whyNot.1: Improvised supports are unsafe and won't keep it accurately positioned.
whyNot.3: Continuing to use faulty equipment risks wrong exposures and retakes.

B.q: If a member of staff ever has to remain in the room during an intraoral exposure, where should they stand?
options: As far away as possible, out of the beam
Close beside the patient, wearing a lead apron
Directly in line with the spacer cone
B.why: The 2020 guidance says anyone who must stay should keep well clear of the main beam and as far from the tubehead and patient as possible. Leaving the controlled area is still the norm.

whyNot.1: Behind the patient's head is in the path of the primary beam.
whyNot.2: Close to the patient is inside the controlled area; an apron is no substitute for distance.
whyNot.3: In line with the cone means standing in the primary beam.

B.q: Which measure reduces patient dose by about half for intraoral radiographs?
options: Wearing a thyroid collar for every view
B.why: Rectangular collimation trims the beam to the receptor size and reduces patient dose by about 50% compared with a round collimator.

whyNot.0: A collar only shields the neck and is not routinely recommended.
whyNot.1: A shorter cone increases skin dose and reduces image sharpness.
whyNot.2: A round beam is larger than the receptor, so it gives more dose.

B.q: When might a thyroid collar be appropriate for a dental patient?
options: When the thyroid is unavoidably in the beam
Whenever the patient or a parent asks for one
B.why: Thyroid shields are used, on MPE advice, only when the thyroid would unavoidably be in the primary beam, such as an upper standard occlusal.

whyNot.0: Bitewings don't put the thyroid in the primary beam, so collars aren't routine.
whyNot.2: Use is based on clinical need and MPE advice, not request alone.
whyNot.3: A collar can block part of a panoramic image; it is only used where the field extends well below the mandible on MPE advice.

C.q: A patient says she might be pregnant before an intraoral radiograph. What is the best initial action?
options: Follow procedure and tell the dentist
Take the radiograph without any comment
C.why: Follow the practice's pregnancy enquiry procedure and inform the dentist, who reviews the justification.

whyNot.0: Cancelling isn't automatic; the dentist decides whether the exposure is still justified.
whyNot.1: Lead aprons are not routinely justified, even in pregnancy.
whyNot.3: Ignoring it bypasses the IR(ME)R pregnancy enquiry procedure.

C.q: Which is the FIRST priority in IRR17's hierarchy of controls?
C.why: IRR17 gives priority to design features and engineering controls such as room layout and shielding.

whyNot.1: PPE is the last resort in the hierarchy.
whyNot.2: Local rules are systems of work, which come after engineering controls.
whyNot.3: Training supports systems of work but isn't the first priority.

C.q: A nurse offers to hold the phosphor plate in a child's mouth during the exposure. What is the correct response?
options: Allow it if she wears an apron
Allow it if the dentist agrees
C.why: Staff must never hold receptors during an exposure; use a holder, or a carer or comforter under a separate justification.

whyNot.0: An apron doesn't protect hands in the primary beam.
whyNot.1: Age makes no difference to the rule for staff.
whyNot.2: A dentist's agreement doesn't make it safe or lawful practice.

reteach.title: Think of a garden sprinkler
reteach.question: Imagine a sprinkler spraying in every direction. How would you avoid getting wet, and how would you water only the plant you want?

blocks.body: To stay dry you'd step well back (distance), stand behind a wall (shielding) and only switch it on briefly (time). That's how staff stay safe: outside the controlled area, behind walls, with short exposures. To water just one plant you'd fit a narrow nozzle and hold it steady. That's the patient's protection: rectangular collimation, holders and a long cone so only the area needed is exposed. A raincoat on the plant's neighbour (an apron) does little when the spray is aimed elsewhere.

blocks.text: Distance beats lead. Leaving the controlled area protects staff far better than wearing an apron beside the chair.

explain.body: It exists whenever the set is ready to expose. Either the whole room (option A), or 1.5 m from tubehead and patient plus the primary beam (option B). For CBCT, the whole room. Staff leave it for every exposure.

test.q: When does the controlled area exist around a dental X-ray set?
options: Only while the patient is seated
When the set is ready to emit X-rays
test.why: The controlled area exists while the equipment is in a state of readiness to emit X-rays; switching it off ends it.

whyNot.0: Patient position doesn't define it; equipment readiness does.
whyNot.1: It exists while the set is ready, not just during the button press.
whyNot.3: Opening hours are irrelevant; it depends on the set being powered and ready.

explain.body: Justify every exposure, then optimise: rectangular collimation, holders with beam aiming devices, paralleling technique, the longer spacer cone, digital receptors and the correct exposure setting.

test.q: Which is NOT a way of optimising the patient's dose?
test.why: Routine lead aprons are not justified for dental radiography; the other options all reduce dose or retakes.

whyNot.0: Holders improve positioning and reduce retakes.
whyNot.1: Rectangular collimation halves dose compared with round.
whyNot.3: Paralleling gives better images at a lower dose than bisecting angle.

explain.body: No routine aprons or thyroid collars. Collars only when the thyroid is unavoidably in the beam, on MPE advice. A possibly pregnant patient: follow the local enquiry procedure and tell the dentist. Pregnant staff: tell the employer.

test.q: Who decides whether an exposure goes ahead when a patient may be pregnant?
test.why: The IR(ME)R practitioner reviews the justification once told about a possible pregnancy.

whyNot.0: Receptionists have no role in justifying exposures.
whyNot.1: The nurse follows the procedure and informs the dentist, but doesn't justify.
whyNot.2: The patient consents, but justification is the practitioner's legal duty.

explain.body: If an exposure won't stop, release the button and switch off at the mains or emergency stop. Any damaged or drifting unit: stop using it, label it, report to the RPS or dentist and follow the contingency plan.

test.q: The 'X-rays' warning light stays on after you release the exposure button. What should you do first?
options: Switch off at the mains or emergency stop
Wait to see if it goes off
Take another exposure to test it
Open the tubehead to look inside
test.why: If X-rays may still be produced, cut the power at the mains or emergency stop straight away, then report it.

whyNot.1: Waiting could prolong an unintended exposure.
whyNot.2: Another exposure adds dose and doesn't fix the fault.
whyNot.3: Only a qualified engineer should open the tubehead.
